**Answer: 9** (from recall of the literature, not derived here)

I could not verify this by a complete argument. The reasoning below only sets up the problem.

**Setup.** Only words of length exactly \(n\) matter, because acceptance of other lengths is unrestricted. So \(E(x)\) is the least number of states of an NFA whose accepting length-\(n\) paths spell exactly \(x\) (with at least one such path). \(U(x)\) is the same minimum with the extra requirement that exactly one accepting path exists. Clearly \(E(x)\le U(x)\) always, so the question is when ambiguity strictly saves states.

**Why the answer is finite.** For short words, a small NFA can usually be made unambiguous without adding states, so \(E(x)=U(x)\). A strict gap needs a word long enough for a state to be reused across layers in a way that creates extra accepting paths, and such a witness is known to exist. The least such length I recall from the literature on nondeterministic and unambiguous state complexity of single words is 9. I have not checked this by exhaustive search, so treat it as unverified.

ANSWER: 9
